opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because I sit in both worlds. I'm a professor at Princeton and I'm also at Together AI, so I see both sides pretty closely.

My view is that they're complementary, and they've always been somewhat complementary, but the balance has shifted. Industry right now has the compute, the data, and the engineering teams to take an idea and scale it up to frontier models. That's something academia just can't do at the same level. If you want to train a model on tens of thousands of GPUs, that's going to happen in industry.

But I think academia has a really important role in exploring ideas that are a bit further out, things that may not pay off for two or three years, or that look a bit unconventional. Industry labs are under pressure to ship and to make the current recipe work a little better. That's very valuable, but it makes it harder to take risks on things that might not work. In academia you have more freedom to say, "What if we tried a completely different architecture?" or "What if we rethink how attention works at the hardware level?" A lot of the ideas that end up mattering started like that, as a small-scale thing that people didn't initially take seriously.

FlashAttention is a good example from my own experience. It started as an academic project, and the question was pretty simple: why is attention slow, and is it really a compute problem or a memory problem? You don't need a giant cluster to study that. You need to understand the hardware and the algorithm. Then industry picked it up very quickly because it solved a real problem for them. That's the ideal flow, I think. Academia finds the idea and shows it works at a reasonable scale, and industry has the resources to push it all the way.

The same is true for things like state space models and alternative architectures. A lot of that exploration happened in academic labs because it was a bit of a bet. Now you see industry adopting hybrid architectures, so those ideas are making their way into production.

The other piece is that academia is where you train people. Many of the best researchers in industry came out of PhD programs where they had the time to go deep on a problem. That pipeline matters a lot.

So I'd say academia should not try to compete with industry on scale. That's a losing game. Academia should focus on ideas that need deep understanding rather than huge compute: new algorithms, new architectures, efficiency, theory, evaluation. Efficiency in particular is a natural fit, because when you have limited resources you're forced to think hard about how to do more with less, and those ideas end up benefiting everyone.

r001.rationale: It describes academia exploring unconventional, longer-term ideas and taking risks on work that may not succeed.

r002.rationale: It does not compare academic research to venture capital investing.

r003.rationale: It discusses FlashAttention’s academic origins but does not say attention originated at Mila before the Google paper.

r004.rationale: It says industry picks up research that solves real problems and pushes it toward production, under pressure to ship.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I've kind of lived on both sides of it. I'm a professor at Princeton, and I'm also chief scientist at Together AI, so I get to see where each side has an advantage and where each side kind of struggles.

The way I think about it is that academia is really good at asking questions that are slightly off the beaten path. In industry, you have a product, you have customers, you have a roadmap, and most of the work has to be in service of that. There's a lot of pressure to do the thing that's going to work in the next three to six months. In academia, you don't have that constraint. You can spend a year or two on something that looks weird, that might not pan out, and that's fine. That's actually the job. So a lot of the ideas that end up mattering, things like attention itself, or a lot of the early work on state space models, those started in settings where nobody was asking "what's the business case for this."

Where industry is really strong is in scale and in engineering. Once you have an idea that seems to work, actually making it work at scale, at thousands of GPUs, with real data, with real latency constraints, that takes a kind of engineering effort and a kind of infrastructure that most academic labs just don't have. And honestly, a lot of the interesting problems only show up at scale. You don't see certain bottlenecks until you're training something big, so there's a feedback loop where industry discovers the problem, and then that problem becomes something academics can go off and think about more carefully.

FlashAttention is kind of an example of that for me. The question came from a very practical pain point, attention was slow and memory-hungry, people were running into it everywhere. But the thing that made it work was sitting down and thinking carefully about the memory hierarchy, which is a fairly academic, systems-y way of looking at the problem. And then the moment it was out, industry picked it up and pushed it much further than I could have on my own.

So I don't really see them as competing. The best setup is when ideas flow in both directions. Academia generates the diversity of approaches, the stuff that's too risky or too early for a company, and industry provides the scale, the real problems, and the validation of what actually matters. The thing I worry about is when the gap in compute gets so large that academics can't even test their ideas at a relevant scale anymore. That's why I think it's important for people in academia to have some connection to industry, and for industry to keep publishing and sharing enough that the ideas can keep flowing back.

r001.rationale: It says academia explores off-the-beaten-path ideas, including approaches that may not pan out, and describes academia as generating a diversity of approaches.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy between academic research and venture capital investing.

r003.rationale: It mentions attention as an idea that began outside business-driven settings, but does not identify Mila or say this preceded the Google paper that popularized it.

r004.rationale: It describes industry as guided by products, customers, roadmaps, and near-term needs, and as taking ideas that work and making them work at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think academia and industry play complementary roles. Industry is very good at taking an idea and making it work at scale. You have the compute, the engineering teams, and the feedback from people actually using the system. And that exposes research problems that might be hard to see from a university.

Academia has more freedom to explore ideas that aren’t obviously useful yet, or to question the assumptions behind what everyone is doing. If you’re a small research group, you probably shouldn’t compete with a big lab on training the largest model. But you can ask whether there’s a better algorithm, whether we’re using the hardware efficiently, or whether a different approach could make these systems much cheaper.

The exciting part is the exchange between the two. Practical constraints can motivate really interesting research, and a research insight can change what’s practical at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says academia can explore ideas that are not obviously useful, but does not characterize this as exploring a broad range despite a low expected success rate.

r002.rationale: It makes no analogy between academic research and venture capital investing or their reliance on a small fraction of ideas succeeding.

r003.rationale: It does not mention attention, Mila, or the timing of academic work relative to the Google paper.

r004.rationale: It describes industry scaling ideas and learning from users, but does not say industry turns promising research into products guided by market needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academia and industry play complementary roles. In academia, you have more freedom to explore ideas that might be risky or might not pay off for several years. You can step back and ask, “Are we approaching this problem the right way?” And a big part of the contribution is training students who then bring those ideas and ways of thinking into industry.

Industry gives you a different kind of feedback. You have real workloads, real users, and constraints that you might not encounter in an academic setting. An idea can look great in a paper, but getting it to work reliably at scale often reveals a whole new set of research problems.

For systems research, especially, I think that interaction is really valuable. You want enough distance to question the assumptions, but enough contact with practice to know which problems matter. Ideally, ideas flow in both directions.

r001.rationale: It describes exploring risky ideas that may take years to pay off, but does not clearly characterize academia as exploring a broad range despite low odds of success.

r002.rationale: It makes no analogy between academic research and venture capital investing.

r003.rationale: It does not mention attention, Mila, or academic work predating the Google paper.

r004.rationale: It describes industry feedback from users, workloads, and scaling constraints, but does not say industry turns promising research into products guided by market needs.
